blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a collection of numbers `candidates` (which **may contain duplicates**) and a `target`, find all unique combinations that add up to `target`. **Each number may be used only once**, and the answer must not contain duplicate combinations.

blocks.alt: candidates sorted: 1, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10 with target 8. The answers are 1+1+6, 1+2+5, 1+7 and 2+6. Starting a combination with the first 1 and with the second 1 would build the same combinations twice, so at the same level the second 1 is skipped. Using both 1s inside one combination, 1+1+6, is still fine.

blocks.text: The idea: Combination Sum, plus Subsets II's skip

Two changes to Combination Sum. Each number is used **once**, so recurse with `i + 1`. And the input has duplicates, so — exactly as in Subsets II — sort it and, at each level, skip a value equal to the one just tried: `if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i − 1]) continue`. The sorted order also gives the pruning `break` when a number is bigger than what's left.
**Time O(n · 2ⁿ).** Fine for 15 numbers; hopeless for 100.

blocks.caption: Each node shows what's still needed; equal values at the same level are skipped, and big ones end the loop.

blocks.text: **Time O(n · 2ⁿ)** in the worst case, **space O(n)**. In practice the sorted `break` and the duplicate skip cut the tree to a small fraction.

blocks.alt: Every subset + filter: O(n · 2^n) time, O(n · 2^n) space. Skip and break: O(n · 2^n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Order of the two checks** — the skip uses `i > start`; the `break` only applies after sorting.
**A value equal to the target** — an answer on its own.
**Combination Sum** — distinct values, unlimited reuse (previous lesson).
**Subsets II** — the same skip without a target.
**Combination Sum III** — k numbers from 1 to 9.
